intro: Open the Qur'an and you meet names many readers already know: Adam, Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Yusuf (Joseph), Musa (Moses), Maryam (Mary) and Isa (Jesus). The Hebrew Bible and the Christian Bible tell about the same figures. Yet the tellings differ. The Qur'an often gives a short scene and assumes its hearers know the rest. Details change, and so does the lesson each book draws. This unit sets passages side by side, Pickthall's 1930 translation of the Qur'an beside the King James Version and the 1917 Jewish Publication Society Bible.

The three traditions have also read one another's books for fourteen centuries. The Qur'an names the Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel. Muslim scholars later argued about whether those texts had been changed. Jewish and Christian writers answered with arguments of their own. In Baghdad and Cordoba, scholars debated in public, and in 1893 Chicago hosted a World's Parliament of Religions. Today, groups of Jews, Christians and Muslims read their scriptures together in study circles.

By the end of this unit you will be able to compare a story as the Qur'an and the Bible tell it, say who believes what about each figure, and explain how each tradition reads the others' books. You will practice comparing without ranking: describing each reading fairly and letting each tradition speak for itself.
bigQuestion: When two scriptures tell the same story differently, how do their readers make sense of the differences?

test.q: Which three earlier books does the Qur'an name?
choices: The Torah, the Psalms and the Gospel
The Talmud, the Mishnah and the Gospel
The Vedas, the Torah and the Psalms
test.why: The Qur'an names the Tawrat (Torah), Zabur (Psalms) and Injil (Gospel).

test.q: In Genesis 22 (KJV), which son is Abraham told to offer?
test.why: Genesis 22:2 names Isaac. The Qur'an (37:102-107) does not name the son there.

test.q: Which son do most Muslim scholars today identify as the son in the sacrifice story of surah 37?
test.why: Most later Muslim scholars say Ismail, though some early commentators said Isaac.

test.q: How do most Muslims read 4:157 about Isa (Jesus)?
choices: He was crucified and rose on the third day
He was not killed or crucified, though it appeared so
test.why: Muslims read 4:157 as saying Isa was not crucified. Christians hold that he was crucified and rose.

test.q: What does the word tahrif mean?
test.why: Tahrif is the Muslim claim that earlier scriptures were changed, in wording or in meaning.

test.q: Some Muslim scholars said tahrif meant changing the meaning, not the words. What is that view?
choices: The Bible was never given by God
Readers twisted how the text was understood
The Psalms were lost at sea
test.why: One strand of scholars held that tahrif was misreading, not rewriting. Others, like Ibn Hazm, argued the words themselves changed.

test.q: Which Qur'an verse says 'For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way'?
test.why: That line is from 5:48 in Surah Al-Ma'idah, in Pickthall's translation.

test.q: Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, says God 'begetteth not nor was begotten.' Which teaching does this express?
test.why: Muslims read surah 112 as a summary of tawhid, and many read it as rejecting the idea that God has a son.

test.q: Where did the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions meet?
test.why: It met in Chicago alongside the World's Columbian Exposition.

test.q: According to the Qur'an (2:127), who raised the foundations of the House, the Kaaba?
test.why: Qur'an 2:127 describes Ibrahim (Abraham) and Ismail raising the foundations of the House.

test.q: Which prophet does the Qur'an call Dhun-Nun, the one of the fish?
test.why: Qur'an 21:87 calls Yunus (Jonah) Dhun-Nun; the Bible tells his story in the Book of Jonah.

test.q: Which statement is a fair, attributed description?
choices: The Bible is right about Jesus
The Qur'an is right about Jesus
Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God; Muslims believe he is a prophet
test.why: A public-school study describes what each tradition believes without saying which is true.

test.q: What does 'People of the Book' mean in the Qur'an?
choices: Jews and Christians, who received earlier scriptures
test.why: The Qur'an uses the phrase for Jews and Christians, as in 3:64.

choices: One faith judges the others' books
Jews, Christians and Muslims study passages from their texts together
Scholars translate the Bible into Arabic
test.why: Scriptural reasoning brings readers of the three traditions to study texts side by side, without asking anyone to agree.

test.q: Why does the Qur'an often tell only part of a story, like Yusuf's or Musa's?
choices: Scholars note it seems to assume hearers already know the story
test.why: Scholars note that the Qur'an often alludes to stories its first hearers knew and focuses on their lesson. Surah 12 is a rare full telling.

write.prompt: Pick one figure the Qur'an and the Bible share: Ibrahim, Musa, Maryam or Isa. How does the Qur'an's telling differ from the Bible's, and how have Muslim, Jewish and Christian readers explained it? Cite two or three passages from the unit (such as Genesis 22, Qur'an 37:102-107, 2:127 or 4:157). Explain what each says and how its readers read it.
tips: Name each text you cite with its book, chapter and verse or surah and ayah.
Attribute every belief: 'Muslims believe', 'Christians hold', 'Jewish commentators read'.
Compare the tellings; do not judge which one is true.
Use unit terms such as tahrif, People of the Book and tafsir.
Note where readers inside one tradition disagree, too.
